metadata.file_name: 107. Tan et al. (2025). Using machine learning algorithms to predict students’ general self-efficacy in PISA 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Using machine learning algorithms to predict students’ general self-efficacy in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 microdata and merges Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire responses at the student–principal level. The analytic sample is created by (i) listwise deletion of cases missing any of the five self-efficacy items and (ii) median imputation for missing predictor values, followed by IRT-based transformation of the five self-efficacy items into a continuous self-efficacy score. The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights or replicate weights in the ML training/evaluation stage, so it is unclear whether population-representative weighting was used. Because the models are XGBoost and Lasso implemented in Python/scikit-learn, the analysis may have proceeded without explicit survey-weight incorporation, which can affect generalizability under clustered sampling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a continuous self-efficacy score derived from five Likert items using an IRT generalized partial credit model and then linearly transformed for interpretability; the paper does not use PISA achievement plausible values for the outcome. Missingness is handled in two stages: listwise deletion for missing self-efficacy items (84,179 records removed) and median substitution for missing predictor values. Because the paper does not describe any PV-based procedure for the outcome, PV handling is not applicable in this analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Start from the publicly available PISA 2018 dataset (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire merged by linking students to their corresponding principals). Exclude any record with missing data on any of the five self-efficacy items, using listwise deletion (reducing the dataset from 612,004 to 527,825). For the remaining cases, impute missing predictor values by substituting median values. Transform the five self-efficacy item responses into IRT-based item response scores using a polytomous generalized partial credit model, then linearly transform the resulting IRT scores (multiply by 15 and add 100) to obtain a positive continuous self-efficacy outcome. Create dummy variables for categorical predictors and reverse-code negatively worded items before computing relevant scale totals.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire), self-efficacy items (general self-efficacy)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (test set): R2 = 0.467; RMSE = 9.699; MAE = 7.219. Lasso (test set): R2 = 0.417; RMSE = 10.137; MAE = 7.683. Best model: XGBoost. Top-14 predictors (XGBoost) cumulative relative importance = 48.99%; reduced model R2 = 0.436 vs full model R2 = 0.467; exclusion model R2 = 0.328.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud emotion, positive emotions, and learning aspiration to predict general self-efficacy (IRT-based continuous score), finding that XGBoost outperformed Lasso and achieved test-set R2 ≈ 0.467 (RMSE ≈ 9.699). This indicates that students’ affective and motivational profiles—along with a small subset of high-importance contextual variables—can support scalable monitoring of self-efficacy, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal pathway claims.

main_findings.target_variable: General self-efficacy (IRT-based continuous score) — top predictors by socio-ecological level
main_findings.performance_metrics: Top predictors by level (relative importance ranking within XGBoost): Microsystem—parents’ emotional support, teacher instruction strategies, study possessions; Mesosystem—cooperation climate, competition climate, teacher evaluation, differentiated classrooms; Exosystem—admission criteria (feeder schools/residence area) and funding sources; Macrosystem—Malaysia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Indonesia, B.S.J.Z. China. Individual-level predictors ranked highest overall; exosystem ranked lowest (based on available predictors).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged parents’ emotional support, teacher instruction strategies, study possessions, cooperation climate, and admission criteria (feeder schools) to predict general self-efficacy, finding that the most influential predictors cluster in proximal socio-ecological layers (especially the individual and microsystem) while exosystem predictors show weaker direct predictive importance. This indicates that interventions aiming to strengthen self-efficacy should prioritize emotional support, instructional practices, and learning-related motivation, while using higher-level policy levers more indirectly through these proximal mechanisms.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata merged from the Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire to predict students’ general self-efficacy. Self-efficacy is constructed from five Likert items using a polytomous IRT generalized partial credit model and then linearly transformed to a positive continuous scale. The authors train two ML regressors—XGBoost and Lasso—using nested cross-validation (4 folds in both inner and outer loops) and evaluate performance with MAE, RMSE, and R². On the test set, XGBoost achieves R² = 0.467 (RMSE = 9.699; MAE = 7.219), outperforming Lasso (R² = 0.417; RMSE = 10.137; MAE = 7.683). The top 14 predictors explain 48.99% of cumulative relative importance, and a reduced model using only these predictors retains substantial explanatory power (R² = 0.436), while an exclusion model drops to R² = 0.328. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal claims) and unclear use of PISA survey weights in the ML stage.
